sections.html:
Worcester is the seat of Worcester County and the largest city in Central Massachusetts, about 40 miles west of Boston and 38 miles northwest of Providence. The 2020 count was 206,518 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 213,862, which makes it the second largest city in the state. Route 146 and Interstates 90, 190, 290, 395 and 495 all serve the area, so many buyers weigh commute access along with the house itself.

A city this size means your house sits among many comparable listings. Condition, age and how easy the street is to reach all shape what buyers and cash investors will pay.

Much of Worcester's housing came out of its factory years. The city grew around canals, railways and mills, and it still has many 19th century triple-decker houses and Victorian-era buildings. Manufacturing faded after World War II, and the population has climbed since the 1990s as healthcare, higher education and biotechnology grew.

  • Triple-deckers are a common building type, and buyers often treat them as small investment properties.
  • Older houses usually come with aging wiring, plumbing, windows and roofs.
  • A cash buyer prices that age and condition into the offer, so you are not asked to fix things before closing.

Worcester gets about 64 inches of snow in an average season and roughly 48 inches of total precipitation a year. The city sits higher than much of the surrounding land and is prone to nor'easters, so roofs, gutters and pipes take a beating.

If you list the house the traditional way, expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at the roof, the gutters and any water stains after a rough winter. If your lot slopes or sits near a pond or brook, say so and mention any past drainage trouble. An as-is sale skips the repair negotiation, which helps when you would rather not pay for work before you sell.

Worcester bills real estate tax four times a year, and each bill is due 30 days after its issue date. The fiscal year runs July 1 through June 30.

BillIssue dateType of bill
First quarterJuly 1Preliminary
Second quarterOctober 1Preliminary
Third quarterJanuary 1Actual
Fourth quarterApril 1Actual

The first two bills are estimates, each equal to the previous year's tax divided by four. The last two are actual bills. They use the new assessment and rate, subtract what was already billed, and split the remainder in two. Any change from reassessment therefore lands in the third and fourth quarters.

Residential and commercial property are taxed at separate rates. The rates posted are $13.28 and $29.06 per $1,000 of assessed value, but no fiscal year is attached, so call Assessing for the rate that applies now. For the statewide rules, see our Massachusetts property tax guide.

The Assessing office is at City Hall, Room 209, 455 Main Street. Call 508-799-1098 or email assessing@worcesterma.gov, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Bring the property address and your latest bill when you call or visit.

  • An abatement is the way to dispute your value or correct a billing error. The city has an online application.
  • Elderly, surviving spouse, blind and disabled veteran exemptions each need an application every year.
  • Owners of apartment and mixed-use buildings are asked to file annual expense forms, which the city treats as private.

Ask the office for the current abatement deadline before you plan around it.

sections.h2: State rules that come up at closing
sections.html:
A Worcester sale follows Massachusetts law. Two state rules come up in almost every closing, and local offices handle the rest.

  • Smoke detectors. M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors on sale or transfer. The head of the fire department enforces it.
  • Deed excise. M.G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the excise at $2 for each $500 of consideration or fraction. Your closing attorney works out the exact figure.
  • Taxes due. Ask the city for the status of every bill before closing so the attorney can pay them from your proceeds.

A cash buyer can purchase a multifamily house with tenants in place. Speak with an attorney early about notices and security deposits, because rules for occupied properties can differ and we do not give legal advice. When you ask for an offer, tell us how many units there are, what each rent is, and whether tenants plan to stay or leave. Those answers change how a buyer values the building.

sections.h2: What a cash sale looks like in Worcester
sections.html:
In a cash sale a buyer purchases the house as is, with no lender to approve. We review the address, condition, tax status and whether tenants live there, then make an offer. You decide whether to accept.

  1. Contact us with the address and a short description of the house.
  2. We review the details and make an offer.
  3. If you accept, a title company or attorney opens the file and checks for liens and unpaid taxes.
  4. At closing, balances owed are paid from the proceeds and you receive the rest.

This route often suits owners who inherited a house they do not want to manage, who live out of state, or who face repair costs they cannot cover before listing. You pick the closing date within a reasonable range. Call or text us and we will say plainly what we can and cannot do for your Worcester house.

faqs.q: How far is Worcester from Boston?
faqs.a: Worcester is about 40 miles west of Boston and 38 miles northwest of Providence, Rhode Island. Interstates 90 and 290 and Route 146 connect it to those cities.

faqs.q: When are Worcester property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Bills are issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days after it is issued. The first two are preliminary and the last two are actual, based on the new assessment.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Worcester assessment?
faqs.a: File a real estate abatement application with the Assessing Division, online or on paper. Call 508-799-1098 for the form and the current filing deadline.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell in Worcester?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors when it is sold or transferred. The head of the fire department enforces the rule.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Worcester triple-decker with tenants?
faqs.a: Yes, a cash buyer can purchase a multifamily house with tenants in place. Talk with an attorney about notice and deposit rules first, and tell us the number of units and the rents when you ask for an offer.
